title: North and South: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Milton and the Mill—Gaskell's Industrial Canvas

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked — a close, loving, and sometimes argumentative look at Elizabeth Gaskell's great industrial novel.
I'm your host, and today we're beginning at the beginning — or rather, at the threshold.
The moment Margaret Hale arrives in Milton-Northern and Gaskell's canvas opens up: smoke, pride, poverty, and an extraordinary cast of characters.
Joining me today are three people whose company I'd want for any long novel, but especially this one.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads fiction the way a watchmaker reads a clock — she sees the mechanism and loves it all the more for that.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels in recorded form than almost anyone alive, and he hears Gaskell's prose the way a musician hears a score — for its rhythm, its timing, its silences.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read North and South as a teenager and has never quite got over it — which is, I think, exactly the right relationship to have with a novel this alive.
Let's begin with the world Gaskell builds — Milton, the north, the mills — and what it means that she chose to set her story here, in this place of smoke and noise and moral friction.
What strikes me first, every time I return to this novel, is how deliberately Gaskell refuses to make Milton picturesque.
So many Victorian novelists, when they write about industry, are essentially writing about it from a carriage window — at a safe aesthetic distance.
Gaskell puts you inside it — inside the smoke, inside the anxiety, inside the bodies of people who are actually breathing cotton-fluff and worrying about wages.
And she does it through Margaret's consciousness, which is a very shrewd structural choice.

Because Margaret arrives as an outsider — a southerner, a clergyman's daughter — she registers everything freshly, even hostilely, which gives Gaskell permission to be honest about how ugly and overwhelming Milton is.
But what I find most daring is that Gaskell then turns the screws on Margaret's very certainties — her southern gentility, her quiet Anglican faith.
By the time we reach the passage where Margaret stands at the window unable to find God in the night sky, we feel how much has already been stripped away from her.
Gaskell writes that those never-ending depths of space, in their still serenity, were more mocking to her than any material bounds could be.
That word 'mocking' — from the infinite silence, no less — is doing extraordinary work.
Eleanor's absolutely right about Margaret as the instrument through which we feel the world — and I'd add that Gaskell is remarkably unsparing about what that world does to a person's interior life.
When I first read that passage aloud in the recording booth, I had to stop.
There's a full sentence in there that just — falls.
The cries of earth's sufferers, Gaskell writes, might ascend into that infinite splendour of vastness and be lost — lost for ever, before they reached His throne.
That repetition of 'lost — lost for ever' — Gaskell is writing for the voice there.
She knows the second 'lost' has to fall into silence, and that the silence is the point.
And then — and this is the craft — the father walks in, unheard, and touches her shoulder.
After all that cosmic vastness, a human touch.
What Oliver just described — that structural movement from the infinite to the intimate — is exactly what makes Gaskell so hard to put down.
She never lets the large themes — faith, class, the condition of England — float free of actual people in rooms, feeling things in their bodies.
And what I find so moving in that passage is that Margaret doesn't resolve anything.
She just — stands there, gazing, and feeling the weight of unanswered prayer.
Gaskell is writing about doubt in a way that I think would have felt genuinely dangerous in 1855.
Not theatrical doubt — not Byron — but quiet, domestic, middle-of-the-night doubt, with your father asleep in the next room.
That texture of the ordinary carrying the extraordinary — it's there from the first pages, isn't it, and it's what makes the social world of the novel feel so charged.
Which brings us to the first collision — because Gaskell wastes very little time before putting Margaret in a room with John Thornton.
Eleanor, can you take us into that early encounter and what Gaskell is setting up there?
It's one of the great first-meeting scenes in Victorian fiction, and what makes it great is that Gaskell refuses to give either character the moral high ground.
Thornton misreads Margaret completely — and yet his misreading is entirely understandable, because what he sees is formidable.
Gaskell gives us this portrait of Margaret almost through Thornton's stunned, resentful gaze — and it is an extraordinary piece of writing.

Her round white flexile throat rising out of the full, yet lithe figure; her lips moving so slightly as she spoke, not breaking the cold serene look of her face with any variation from the one lovely haughty curve.
'Flexile' — that's the word I keep returning to.
It means supple, yielding — but everything else in the description is unyielding, cold, serene.
Gaskell is encoding the contradiction of Margaret — the softness that is also, somehow, steel — in a single adjective.
And Thornton's response to all of this — to this vision of loveliness that refuses to notice him — is almost comic in its wounded male pride.
He almost said to himself that he did not like her — Gaskell's italics, not mine — before their conversation ended.
'Almost said to himself' — meaning he couldn't quite manage it, even as self-protection.
The man is already lost and he doesn't know it yet.

What I love is that Gaskell tells us Margaret's bearing always gave strangers the impression of haughtiness — and then immediately tells us she's simply tired and would rather not be making conversation at all.
The comedy of misreading, played perfectly straight.
And yet there's something I want to push back on slightly — because I don't think it's only comedy.
Margaret's coldness in that scene is also genuine.
She does think he's rough and unpolished — Gaskell tells us that plainly.
And what's so interesting is that her first real thaw comes not when Thornton is impressive, but when he is simple.
Later, when he's admitted to having been a shop-boy, Margaret says something to her father that I find enormously telling.

Everything else revolted me, from its hardness; but he spoke about himself so simply — with so little of the pretence that makes the vulgarity of shop-people, and with such tender respect for his mother.
'Tender respect for his mother' — that's what gets through to Margaret where Milton's grandeur entirely failed.
That's such a sharp observation — because it shows us that Margaret's snobbery, if we want to call it that, isn't really about class at all.
It's about a kind of moral texture — authenticity, humility, the willingness to acknowledge where you came from.
Thornton boasting about Milton, quietly despising those he considers improvident — that repels her.
Thornton speaking of his mother with tenderness — that, for the first time, makes him human in her eyes.
Gaskell is using this not just to show us Margaret's values, but to prepare us — structurally — for the long, painful education both characters are about to undergo.
That word 'education' feels exactly right — and it points toward everything we're going to be exploring in the episodes to come.
Two people who think they understand the world, gradually discovering they don't — and finding each other in the gap.
A warm thank you to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for setting us so beautifully on our way.
In our next segment, we'll be going deeper into the mills — into labour, power, and the figure of Thornton as Gaskell's great portrait of industrial capitalism at its most human and most flawed.

segments.title: Margaret's Journey: From South to North, Innocence to Agency

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're following one of the great character journeys in Victorian fiction.
Margaret Hale arrives in Milton as a vicar's daughter from the soft Hampshire countryside — and she leaves something altogether different.
We're going to trace that transformation today, through some very close reading of Gaskell's prose.
Joining me are three wonderful readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and thinks about novels the way a watchmaker thinks about movements — she wants to know exactly which gear is doing what.
Oliver Trevelyan has read more classic novels aloud than almost anyone alive, and he hears things in Gaskell's sentences that the rest of us miss on the page.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read North and South as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since.
Let's start at the tea-table in Chapter Ten — because Gaskell plants everything there.
The tea scene is one of those passages I'd perform if someone gave me twenty minutes and an audience.
Gaskell is doing something almost impossibly nimble here — comedy, social observation, and the first true tremor of attraction, all at once.
Thornton cannot stop watching this bracelet slide down Margaret's wrist and fall.
And Gaskell gives us his interiority in this wonderfully undignified little voice:
"He could almost have exclaimed — 'There it goes again!'"
This is the most powerful man in Milton reduced to an internal squeak of delight over a piece of jewellery.
Gaskell is laughing, gently, at both of them.
What strikes me about that passage is how much Gaskell does through focalization.
We are entirely in Thornton's point of view — Margaret is being watched, catalogued, desired — and yet she has her own counter-narrative running simultaneously.
Because Gaskell tells us Margaret has a headache, and she is resolved — and this is the word —
"to throw herself into the breach, if there was any long untoward pause, rather than that her father's friend, pupil, and guest should have cause to think himself in any way neglected."
She is performing duty under physical suffering, and no one in the room knows it.
Gaskell is already building the architecture of Margaret's agency — she acts, she chooses, even when it costs her.
And then comes the sugar-tongs moment, which I find almost unbearably tender.
Her father takes her little finger and thumb in his hand to use them as sugar-tongs.
And Thornton watches her eyes in that moment — Gaskell writes:
"her beautiful eyes lifted to her father, full of light, half-laughter, and half-love."
That hyphenated phrase — half-laughter and half-love — is doing so much work.
It tells us who Margaret is before she's been given a single line of debate or moral argument.
And yet within the very same chapter, that warmth gets weaponised.
Because Margaret — that same woman performing graceful hostess duty with a headache — erupts in defence of the South.
This is the passage I return to most often in the early chapters.
Because Margaret is genuinely angry — Gaskell says she has angry tears in her eyes.
But the argument she makes is not sentimental — it's precise and devastating.
She says — and I want to read this properly:
"I see men here going about in the streets who look ground down by some pinching sorrow or care — who are not only sufferers but haters."
Not only sufferers but haters.
That distinction is morally and politically exact — and she's a girl who has been in Milton for what, a few weeks?
And she knows she's gone too far — which makes it even better.
Gaskell writes that she concludes by "collapsing into a determined silence, and angry with herself for having said so much."
The comedy of that — the passion, the magnificent overreach, and then the immediate self-reproach — it's a complete human being in three lines.
And the full passage before that collapse is worth hearing.
"There is not that terrible expression in their countenances of a sullen sense of injustice which I see here."
Sullen sense of injustice — she has named something that most social commentators of her time wouldn't find the words for.
What I want to hold alongside this is what Thornton says as he leaves the house.
Because Gaskell gives us the most delicious example of a man protesting too much.
He mutters to himself:
"A more proud, disagreeable girl I never saw. Even her great beauty is blotted out of one's memory by her scornful ways."
He acknowledges her great beauty in the very sentence where he claims to have forgotten it.
Gaskell's structural wit is right there in the grammar — he can't even lie to himself without the lie undoing itself.
That self-betrayal in the grammar — it's wonderful.
But I want to move us from Margaret's public voice to her private life — because Chapter Eleven shows us another kind of transformation entirely.
This is the chapter where we first understand that Mrs. Hale is seriously ill — and Gaskell is heartbreakingly subtle about it.
Margaret doesn't know the truth yet.
She catches only a fragment — she goes into her mother's room and finds her on her knees.
And Gaskell is very precise about what Margaret overhears:
"she caught a few words which were evidently a prayer for strength and patience to endure severe bodily suffering."
A few words.
Not the prayer itself — just the shape of it, glimpsed and terrible.
That restraint is the key to everything Gaskell does with grief in this novel.
She never gives us the full catastrophe — she gives us the door just closing, the overheard fragment.
And what it does to Margaret's interiority is extraordinary.
Gaskell writes that Margaret lies awake planning how to reduce the burden on her mother — not weeping, not despairing, planning.
That is Gaskell's Margaret — the emotional weight converts immediately into purposeful action.
And the Milton air itself becomes a kind of antagonist in that chapter.
Gaskell describes it as — and this is wonderful — "deprived of all revivifying principle."
There's something almost gothic about that phrase — air that cannot revive, that takes rather than gives.
And it reminds us that the North isn't just a social challenge for the Hales — it's a physical one.
Let's jump forward now to Chapter Twenty-Seven, where Thornton appears at the Hale house — uninvited, urgent, carrying fruit for Mrs. Hale.
Eleanor, this passage has always struck me as one of Gaskell's most carefully engineered entrances.
It is almost architectural in its precision.
Gaskell gives us the physical approach first — he goes at an unusual pace, he goes upstairs two steps at a time.
The rhythm of the prose is doing the work of the body — we feel the urgency before we see the face.
And then she lands the image:
"his face flushed, his eyes shining with kindly earnestness."
Kindly earnestness — not passion, not desire — kindness.
Gaskell is showing us the full Thornton here — the man who can be tender without being sentimental.
And the narrative note that follows that image is the one I'd want to read aloud in any performance.
Gaskell tells us plainly: "Her heart fluttered, if his did not at this interview."
The conditional — if his did not — is masterful.
We know perfectly well his heart is hammering.
But he takes no notice of her — he goes straight to Mrs. Hale — and that is the measure of him.
That phrase — in that subdued and gentle tone which is so touching when used by a robust man in full health, speaking to a feeble invalid — stays with me.
Gaskell is registering the physical contrast almost as a moral one.
His health and strength brought into the service of her fragility.
And Margaret watches all of this — standing off to one side — and she cannot look away.
And the final passage I want us to consider today marks perhaps the most private moment in Margaret's journey — the grief after her father's death, when her aunt arrives.
Eleanor, you've written about this passage before.
It's the passage where Gaskell earns everything she's built across forty chapters.
Margaret has been described in the scene as white, motionless, speechless, tearless.
Four adjectives, all negatives in effect.
She has been stripped of response — and then her aunt walks in.
And Gaskell explains why a single embrace undoes her:
"All thoughts of quiet habitual love, of tenderness for years, of relationship to the dead, all that inexplicable likeness in look, tone, and gesture, that seem to belong to one family —"
"came in to melt and soften her numbed heart into the overflow of warm tears."
The overflow of warm tears — that phrase is so physiologically exact.
There's a detail just before this that I find almost funny in the most human way.
Poor Mr. Bell has been urging Margaret to eat — sweetbreads stewed with oysters — and she keeps refusing.
And Gaskell adds: "he was obliged to console himself for her rejection, by eating them all himself."
Even in a scene of extreme grief, Gaskell will not abandon us to pure darkness.
She keeps the world going — appetite, comedy, the small consolations of stewed oysters.
What moves me most about that passage is the phrase relationship to the dead.
The aunt is a living connection to Margaret's mother — she carries the physical family resemblance.
And it's that inexplicable likeness in look, tone, and gesture that breaks Margaret open.
Not a speech, not a memory — a gesture.
Grief arriving through the body, through resemblance.
Gaskell understands how we actually lose people — and how we find them again, briefly, in the living faces of those they loved.
That's a beautiful place to pause.
From the bracelet falling at the tea-table to warm tears overflowing in a bereaved daughter's arms — Gaskell has taken us a long way in these passages today.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at how Gaskell constructs the industrial world that forms the backdrop — and very often the engine — of all these private transformations.
Thank you, Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — back in a moment.

segments.title: The Laughter in the Darkness: Wit and Survival in Industrial England

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three readers who know this novel with uncommon intimacy.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Gaskell the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — for the hidden engineering beneath the surface.
Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels than perhaps any other voice actor alive, and he hears prose the way a musician hears a score — for rhythm, timing, and what the silence does.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read North and South as a teenager and has returned to it ever since — she knows exactly where it breaks your heart and exactly where it makes you laugh.
Today's subject is wit — how Gaskell uses humour and irony not as decoration but as survival equipment in a world of industrial hardship and class collision.
Oliver, you've spent a great deal of time with this novel in the recording booth.
Where do you find Gaskell's comic sensibility most alive?
In the moments of wounded pride, without question.
There's a scene early on where Thornton confesses to his mother — with what Gaskell calls a short scornful laugh — that Margaret Hale has not exactly welcomed him into her esteem.
And he delivers his own humiliation with this magnificent, self-lacerating precision.
He says, and I have to read this because the phrasing is extraordinary —
"she treated me with a haughty civility which had a strong flavour of contempt in it.
She held herself aloof from me as if she had been a queen, and I her humble, unwashed vassal."
Unwashed vassal.
He's writing his own comedy of mortification, and he knows it, and he cannot quite stop himself.
That's Gaskell's genius — the joke and the sting are the same thing.
What strikes me about that moment is the structure of it — the parenthetical stage direction Gaskell inserts: "with a short scornful laugh."
She's not just giving us dialogue — she's giving us the performance of the dialogue.
Thornton is narrating his own wound with a kind of bitter relish that tells us everything about his character before the story has properly started.
And what's architecturally brilliant is that Gaskell immediately undercuts the comedy — "Be easy, mother" — as if he can hear himself and wants to close the door on it.
The laugh and the retreat happen in the same breath.
And for a reader who already loves Margaret, there's a delicious irony in hearing Thornton describe her condescension.
Because we know Margaret isn't actually cruel — she is simply southern, and proud, and displaced.
The word "unwashed" is doing extraordinary work.
He is a manufacturer, self-made, and he knows precisely the social charge behind that word — he's almost daring his mother to argue with him.
And then not long after, Gaskell gives us a portrait of Thornton that is almost the opposite of comic — it is a study in contained power.
Margaret is watching him alongside her father — soft, literary, gentle Mr. Hale — and the contrast is almost painterly.
Gaskell writes —
"The straight brows fell low over the clear, deep-set, earnest eyes, which without being unpleasantly sharp, seemed intent enough to penetrate into the very heart and core of what he was looking at."
Penetrate into the very heart and core.
This is not a comfortable gaze to be under — and Margaret feels it, even when she thinks she's immune to it.
The contrast Gaskell builds there is structurally quite masterful.
Mr. Hale's face is described as soft and waving, with fluctuating emotion — almost liquid.
Then Thornton's lines are few but firm, as if carved in marble.
She's using physiognomy as argument — these faces are thesis statements about North and South.
And then she does something unexpected — she gives Thornton a smile, a rare bright smile, and likens its suddenness to a child's.
That one detail cracks open the marble, and Margaret notices it.
It's the first thing she says she admired in him.
Gaskell gives us that very quietly — "Margaret liked this smile" — almost a throwaway line.
But for a reader who knows where this story goes, it's the pin that the whole novel is hung on.
I want to bring in Nicholas Higgins here, because wit in this novel isn't confined to the drawing room.
Oliver, you've talked about Higgins's voice — and there's a passage in chapter seventeen that I think crystallises something important about how Gaskell frames working-class argument.
Higgins is one of the great voices in Victorian fiction and he is almost always underestimated.
There's a moment where he turns to Margaret — young wench, he calls her, with deep affection — and dismantles her assumptions about the strike.
He lists his household — Bessy, and Mary, and himself — on sixteen shillings a week, and then he pivots.
He says —
"I take up John Boucher's cause, as lives next door but one, wi' a sickly wife, and eight childer, none on 'em factory age;
and I don't take up his cause only, though he's a poor good-for-nought, as can only manage two looms at a time, but I take up th' cause o' justice.
Why are we to have less wage now, I ask, than two year ago?"
That final question lands like a hammer.
He has just moved from the personal to the political in four sentences, and the logic is absolutely airtight.
And the grim laugh at the top of that speech — he laughed grimly — sets the register perfectly.
This is not bitterness without intelligence.
It's the laugh of someone who has been patient with a world that isn't patient with him, and who now has to explain the obvious to someone he likes.
There's real tenderness toward Margaret in that speech, and also a kind of exasperation.
What Gaskell is doing with Higgins's dialect is politically courageous for its moment.
She renders his speech phonetically — not to mock him, but to honour the specificity of his voice.
The argument he makes is as rigorous as anything spoken in the Hale drawing room — perhaps more so.
The form of the speech and the dignity of the speaker are inseparable.
Let's turn now to a very different kind of comedy — the comedy of involuntary feeling.
Oliver, there's a passage at the Thornton dinner where John enters and cannot — quite literally cannot — stop looking at Margaret.
This passage is everything.
Thornton enters, shakes Margaret's hand — and Gaskell notes that he knew it was the first time their hands had met, though she was perfectly unconscious of the fact.
That asymmetry is quietly devastating.
And then he looks at Fanny, and he looks at Margaret, and Gaskell gives us this extraordinary comparison —
"he saw his sister's restless way of continually arranging some part of her gown, her wandering eyes, now glancing here, now there, but without any purpose in her observation;
and he contrasted them uneasily with the large soft eyes that looked forth steadily at one object, as if from out their light beamed some gentle influence of repose."
And then he sighs.
He takes it all in with one of his sudden comprehensive glances — and then turns his back on her, and throws himself into a conversation with Mr. Hale.
"With an effort, but with all his heart and soul" — that qualification is heartbreaking.
He has to physically wrench himself away from looking at her.
And the comedy lies in how controlled he appears to everyone else in that room.
The Fanny comparison is so precisely mean — in the best possible way.
Gaskell doesn't simply say Margaret is beautiful and composed — she shows it by contrast with restless, arrangement-obsessed Fanny.
The satire and the tenderness are working simultaneously, in the same sentence.
And then Gaskell delivers what I think is one of the funniest lines in the novel — from chapter twenty-seven.
Margaret is trying to be invisible — she thinks Thornton hasn't noticed her in the room.
She was half afraid of making any noise to arouse him into a consciousness of her being in the room.
And then Gaskell inserts her authorial voice like a blade —
"As if he did not feel the consciousness of her presence all over, though his eyes had never rested on her!"
That exclamation mark.
Gaskell is laughing — warmly, tenderly, but laughing — at the magnificent self-deception of two people who cannot look directly at each other.
It's the narrator winking at the reader over the characters' heads.
And it works because we are entirely on Thornton's side at this point — we know what Margaret cannot yet admit.
So the comedy is also suspense.
That instinct — to hold two emotional registers at once, the comic and the aching — seems to be one of Gaskell's most distinctive gifts in this novel.
Thank you all — Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — this has been a rich and genuinely delightful conversation.
Next time we'll be turning to the novel's treatment of illness, grief, and the domestic interior — the quieter catastrophes.

segments.title: Thornton's Reckoning: Capital, Conscience, and the Strike

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We've been living with the Hales as they settle into Milton — and now the novel turns its full attention to Thornton.
Not simply as a suitor, but as a man whose entire identity is built from commerce — and who is beginning, slowly, to be cracked open by it.
Today we're examining what Gaskell does with capital, conscience, and the strike — the passages where Thornton is seen, assessed, and begins to see himself differently.
Eleanor Hartley is here — she's our literary architect, always alert to how the novel's structure does its moral work.
Oliver Trevelyan joins us — he's narrated more classic fiction than anyone I know, and he hears Gaskell's prose the way a musician hears a score.
And Caroline Woodcourt is with us — a lifelong reader of Gaskell who has an unerring instinct for when the novel is doing something quietly extraordinary.
Let's begin with first impressions — specifically, Margaret's.
What strikes me every time I return to those early chapters is the precision of Margaret's eye.
She is trying to be fair to Thornton — trying quite hard, actually — and what comes out is something more revealing than a simple compliment.
She tells her mother — and this is almost a verdict — that
"With such an expression of resolution and power, no face, however plain in feature, could be either vulgar or common."
The syntax is doing so much work there.
She begins with the concession — plain, possibly common — and then the force of his character simply overrules it.
And then she adds: "I should not like to have to bargain with him."
Which is — for a woman who is constitutionally incapable of backing down — rather a large admission.
That phrase — "sagacious, and strong, as becomes a great tradesman" — is where Gaskell is being quietly satirical and quite affectionate at the same time.
Margaret is bestowing praise — real praise — but she's bracketing it with "tradesman."
She can see exactly what he is and cannot quite decide whether that thing is admirable or slightly beneath her.
That tension is the engine of the whole novel, really.
And what's structurally bold is that Gaskell lets Margaret articulate this judgment so clearly, so early.
We know immediately where she stands — and so the whole arc of the book becomes about dismantling that position from the inside.
"A man who seems made for his niche."
I've always felt that line has a faint whiff of the naturalist about it — as if Margaret is classifying a particularly impressive specimen.
She is not unimpressed — she is very impressed — but she would like it noted that she is observing from a slight elevation.
What I find irresistible as a reader aloud is that word "inflexible."
It's a warning she's issuing to herself.
And yet Margaret's initial condescension — the "poor fellow, he can't help being in trade" — is even more pointed when Mrs. Hale pushes back.
There's a remarkable little speech in chapter nine where we see Margaret actually defending Thornton — while still talking down to him, in a sense.
That passage is one of the moments I return to whenever I want to show students how dramatic irony and character revelation can occupy the same sentence.
Margaret is exhausted, and the exhaustion lowers her guard just enough.
She insists on her own dignity first — and this is the line I love:
"I am myself a born and bred lady through it all, even though it comes to scouring a floor, or washing dishes."
The self-assertion there is absolute — almost regal.
And then comes the deflation: "I don't suppose his education would fit him for much else."
She has defended him, pitied him, and slightly insulted him all in one breath.
"Poor fellow" — that tiny phrase — I cannot tell you how much pleasure it gives me every time.
She is speaking of a man who at that very moment is probably staring down striking workers with complete composure.
And yet Margaret speaks of him as if he needs her sympathy.
Gaskell's comedy is so discreet — there are no nudges — but it's all there.
What moves me in that passage is the last line — Gaskell adds it so quietly.
"Margaret lifted herself slowly up, and went to her own room; for just now she could not bear much more."
Everything Margaret will not say aloud is in that walk across the room.
The comedy and the tenderness live right next to each other here — which is very Gaskell.
While Margaret is composing her studied indifference, someone else has a far less ambivalent view of Thornton entirely.
Mrs. Thornton — whose devotion to her son is possibly the most combustible force in the novel.
I adore Mrs. Thornton with my whole heart, and I won't apologise for it.
That speech she delivers — almost entirely to herself, which is the funniest detail — is a masterclass in concentrated fury.
She begins with outrage — "Despise my son! treat him as her vassal, indeed!" — and then arrives at something almost tender:
"Boy and man, he's the noblest, stoutest heart I ever knew."
That rhythm — "Boy and man" — is pure oral tradition.
It's the kind of sentence that sounds like a ballad.
And then she crashes back to earth: "I hate her!"
The self-correction she performs in the middle of her own rant is what I find so striking.
"I don't care if I am his mother; I can see what's what, and not be blind."
She knows the objection — of course a mother would say that — and she overrides it before anyone else can raise it.
There's something almost legal about it.
And then the contrast with Fanny — "I know what Fanny is; and I know what John is" — that dry parallel says everything in six words.
Mrs. Thornton is one of those characters who could so easily become a villain, and Gaskell simply refuses to let that happen.
The pride is real, the love is real, and the narrowness is real — and you cannot extract one from the others.
She functions structurally as a mirror for Thornton — she represents the ideology he has absorbed and is slowly beginning to outgrow.
And that outgrowing — that transformation — is exactly what we see examined so piercingly later.
Because there's a passage in chapter fifty that gives us the fullest account we have of what Thornton was — and what he is becoming.
That chapter fifty passage is extraordinary — it's one of the great passages of Victorian fiction for understanding how ideology inhabits a person.
Gaskell gives us Thornton's founding myth — the merchant prince, the self-made man — in all its genuine grandeur.
She doesn't mock it.
His mother reads scripture to him as a child — "Her merchants be like princes" — as if it were a trumpet-call.
But the architecture of the passage performs the problem: all that grandeur is pointed outward — to foreign countries, far-away seas — and nowhere near his own people.
"He and they had led parallel lives — very close, but never touching."
That sentence is the whole novel in miniature.
And then Higgins.
The accident — and Gaskell puts that word in parentheses, which I think is deliberate and rather mischievous — of knowing one man.
Not workers as a class, not labour as an abstraction — one individual.
And it's through that one face-to-face meeting that the line comes — and it's the line at the heart of everything in this novel:
"We have all of us one human heart."
Gaskell attributes it quietly — it's spoken as a recognition, not a proclamation.
Which makes it all the more devastating.
When you read that passage aloud, the rhythm of it is almost geological — these long, slow sentences building up strata of context.
Gaskell is building the full weight of Thornton's ambition — all those foreign countries and far-away seas — and then she releases it all with a single clause.
"Strange, shrewd, ignorant; but, above all, full of character and strong human feeling."
That final clause — "strong human feeling" — arrives like a door opening.
The novel has been waiting for Thornton to walk through it — and here he finally does.
And yet before that door fully opens, we need to return to the riot — and to the extraordinary scene where Margaret steps in front of the crowd.
Because what follows — Margaret's private reckoning with what she's done — is one of the most searingly honest passages in the book.
This is the passage I would point to if someone asked me what Gaskell can do that almost no other Victorian novelist can quite match.
The self-examination Margaret performs here is not tidy.
It lurches — she argues herself out of guilt, and then argues herself back in, within the same paragraph.
And the self-condemnation she reserves for herself is written at the exact pitch of her own voice:
"I, who hate scenes — I, who have despised people for showing emotion — who have thought them wanting in self-control — I went down and must needs throw myself into the melée, like a romantic fool!"
The triple build — "I, who... I, who... I" — is almost Shakespearean in its accumulation.
And then the hammer: "like a romantic fool."
She is using her own standards to convict herself — which is the most painful kind of self-criticism there is.
The shame in that passage is physical — and Gaskell insists on the body.
"Her pale cheeks suddenly became one flame of fire; and she covered her face with her hands."
You can feel the heat of it.
And then: "When she took them away, her palms were wet with scalding tears."
"Scalding" is such a precise word.
Not weeping, not crying — scalding.
The emotion burns because it cannot yet be admitted even to herself.
There's a moment in that passage where the narrator gently intervenes — "as in an instant her well-poised judgment felt" — after Margaret has argued herself too far in the wrong direction.
It's Gaskell doing something a touch theatrical — holding Margaret to account even in her private thoughts.
And then there's the moment Margaret catches herself insisting "I in love — and with him too!"
The vehemence of that denial is — well — it's the oldest tell in literature.
The more emphatically she insists it's impossible, the more entirely obvious it becomes.
And what is remarkable is that both characters — Thornton and Margaret — are undergoing their reckonings simultaneously, in parallel, and in profound ignorance of each other.
Gaskell holds these two trajectories apart with extraordinary patience before letting them converge.
We'll pick up that thread in our next segment — where we look at what it costs both of them to finally speak.

segments.title: Higgins Unbound: Working-Class Dignity and Solidarity

utterances.text: Welcome back to North and South Unpacked.
We've spent time with the drawing rooms and the mill offices — now we're turning to the streets of Milton.
Specifically, to the figures who make those streets alive: Nicholas Higgins, his daughter Bessy, and the tentative, extraordinary connection that forms between them and Margaret Hale.
Eleanor, as someone who thinks deeply about how novelists build their effects from the ground up — what does Gaskell do in these early Higgins scenes that strikes you as structurally remarkable?
What strikes me immediately is that Gaskell doesn't introduce Higgins through a dramatic confrontation or a formal presentation.
She smuggles him in — almost accidentally — through a street compliment.
And the compliment itself is doing so much work.
The text reads:
"You may well smile, my lass; many a one would smile to have such a bonny face."
Now — that man is described as careworn.
He is worn down, diminished — and yet he notices beauty and offers it back to her freely, without expectation.
Gaskell is already saying: poverty does not strip a man of his capacity for grace.
And what I love as a performer is the silence that follows that compliment.
Gaskell writes that "a silent recognition was established between them whenever the chances of the day brought them across each other's paths."
They never exchange a word beyond that first compliment — and yet she regards him with more interest than anyone else in Milton.
For a performer, that is a magnificent instruction: play the pause, not the speech.
Gaskell understood that genuine connection is often made in the space between words.
And then comes the flowers scene — which breaks my heart every time, in the best way.
Margaret has gathered dog-violets and lesser celandines from the fields on the edge of town.
Gaskell describes it as gathered with "an unspoken lament in her heart for the sweet profusion of the South."
So the flowers already carry homesickness, longing — and she gives them away.
And the girl's "pale blue eyes lightened up" as she takes them.
That one image — those pale, sickly eyes catching light — does the work of a paragraph.
Caroline, yes — and notice what Gaskell is doing architecturally with the South-North opposition in that moment.
The flowers are literally the South — gathered from fields at the edge of the industrial town, where nature still persists, thinly.
Margaret giving them to Bessy is her offering the South to the North — her world to theirs.
And crucially, it's an impulse — not a considered act of charity, but a spontaneous human gesture.
Gaskell is very deliberate about that: Margaret is not performing benevolence, she is simply responding.
And the father speaks for the daughter — which is its own small drama.
Bessy's gratitude is mediated through him, through that working-class voice.
What I find wonderful is the consequence Gaskell draws from all of this.
She writes:
"Milton became a brighter place to her. It was that in it she had found a human interest."
Not the spring light, not the passage of time — a human interest.
Gaskell is making a profound claim: that place only becomes home through persons.
That line always stops me.
It's so quietly stated, and so completely true to how we actually experience belonging.
And it pays off at the very end of the novel — which I find extraordinarily moving.
Thornton tells Margaret about a round-robin petition from his men.
"I had a round-robin from some of my men — I suspect in Higgins' handwriting — stating their wish to work for me, if ever I was in a position to employ men again on my own behalf."
Higgins — who fought Thornton, who clashed with him, who buried his daughter — writes that petition.
That is what solidarity looks like in this novel: not sentiment, but action, taken in full knowledge of the cost.
And the detail of the handwriting — "I suspect in Higgins' handwriting" — is Gaskell being wonderfully precise about how class and literacy intersect.
Higgins is the one who can write — who has educated himself, who has the language.
He becomes the voice of his community in the most literal sense: he holds the pen.
And there is a thread — unbroken — from that careworn man on the street offering a smile to Margaret, to the man who drafts a petition of loyalty years later.
Gaskell builds her characters through accumulation — each small gesture is a brick.
That image of the unbroken thread is a beautiful place to pause.
From a street compliment in early spring, through wildflowers and pale eyes catching light, all the way to a petition written in a recognisable hand.
Gaskell traces the moral life of Milton through exactly these accumulations — small dignities held together across a novel.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at the language of industrial conflict — the strikes, the violence, and what Gaskell risks in her portrayal of power on both sides.

segments.title: The Gap Between Worlds: Narrative Distance and Moral Ambiguity

utterances.text: Welcome to North and South Unpacked.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the most quietly extraordinary aspects of Elizabeth Gaskell's novel — the way it uses narrative distance to carry enormous moral weight.
We have three brilliant readers with us, and I want to introduce them properly, because each brings something the others can't.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who lives inside the architecture of great prose — the way a sentence is built, the way an image carries a chapter.
She sees Gaskell's craft choices with the eye of someone who makes the same choices herself.

Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels for audio than almost anyone alive, and he approaches every text as a performer — he hears the rhythms, the comic timing, the silences written into the prose.
He is also, it should be said, one of the more entertaining people you'll meet.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
She reads with the intimacy of someone for whom these characters are genuinely real, and she has strong opinions about who deserves better from the plot.
Today's segment takes us across some of the novel's most charged passages — moments where the narrator's distance from the action becomes, paradoxically, the source of its deepest feeling.
Eleanor, I want to start with you — and with the nursery scene right at the opening of the novel.
That nursery scene is one of Gaskell's great sleights of hand, and I think it's underrated simply because it comes so early.
We're in the room with Margaret at eighteen, looking around the nursery she first entered nine years before — and the narrator gives us both ages simultaneously.
The phrase Gaskell uses to describe nine-year-old Margaret arriving in London is quite extraordinary.
She writes that Margaret was brought, quote, 'all untamed from the forest.'
That is not naturalistic description — that is a fairy-tale frame dropped into a social novel.
It tells you everything about how Margaret is going to move through every room she enters — as a creature from somewhere else, carrying different air.
And then there's the beautiful spatial disorientation of the child who can't place herself in the house's vertical geography.
Her father and aunt are dining somewhere far below, 'an infinite depth of stairs' — she thinks they must be in 'the bowels of the earth.'
That is the child's terror rendered as comedy — but barely.
That vertical axis — heaven above, the bowels of the earth below — it's practically a Dante diagram of the English class system.
The nurse is upstairs keeping everything clean and ceremonious, the grown-ups are somewhere unreachably below, and the child is marooned in the middle.
And what I notice as a reader of the prose aloud is the terrible compression in the next few sentences.
Gaskell writes of 'the tears shed with such wild passion of grief by the little girl of nine' — and then immediately, in the same breath, the child suppresses all of it to protect her father.
She hides under the bedclothes crying, is told to stop because it will disturb Edith, and then goes on crying more quietly.
That is Margaret Hale's entire moral education in miniature — contain yourself for others, grieve in silence, and never make your father unhappy.
She's nine years old and she's already performing emotional labour for the adults in the room.
What strikes me, re-reading it, is that Gaskell says Margaret 'rather thought it was wrong to feel' her grief at all.
Not that she was told it was wrong — she had internalised that.
At nine years old.
And the reason she thinks it's wrong is beautifully specific — because of all 'the long hoping, and planning, and contriving they had gone through at home' to get her there.
Her family has sacrificed for this opportunity. She must not waste it with tears.
The whole novel is in that detail — Margaret perpetually holding herself accountable to other people's investment in her.
And that structure gets tested at its absolute limit in the mill-yard scene in Chapter Twenty-Two.
Because there, Margaret acts — genuinely, bodily acts — and the narrator renders it with this extraordinary gothic compression.
The sentence is barely three lines long and it contains a wound, a death-like collapse, and a kind of resurrection.
Listen to the precision of it:
'A sharp pebble flew by her, grazing forehead and cheek, and drawing a blinding sheet of light before her eyes.'
That 'blinding sheet of light' — it's not just physical shock.
It's a near-visionary moment — the body overwhelmed, consciousness dissolving — and Gaskell gives it to us in a single subordinate clause.
And then: 'She lay like one dead on Mr. Thornton's shoulder.'
'Like one dead' — not dead. The simile does so much work.
Every time I've read that passage aloud, I find myself slowing almost to a stop on 'like one dead.'
Because Gaskell is doing something extremely clever — she's giving us the image of the pietà, the body cradled after sacrifice, and she immediately follows it with Thornton unfolding his arms.
He 'held her encircled in one for an instant' — and the passage ends there, mid-gesture.
Mid-gesture. The narrator cuts away.
That is an almost cinematic piece of restraint from a novelist writing in 1855.
The most charged moment of physical contact in the novel, and Gaskell shows us the frame around it and then refuses to fill it in.
It's a scene I've re-read many times, and what I keep returning to is what it costs Margaret.
She steps forward to shield Thornton from the mob — an extraordinary act — and she pays for it with blood and public humiliation.
And the novel immediately makes her sacrifice socially ambiguous — people assume the worst of her motives.
That is a deeply uncomfortable thing for Gaskell to do to her heroine, and I think it's one of the braver choices in the book.
I want to bring in Nicholas Higgins here, because he offers us a very different mode of moral expression in the novel — blunt, material, entirely without sentiment.
Eleanor, you've been assigned his great statement of creed in Chapter Eleven — what do you make of it?
Higgins is one of Gaskell's great ventriloquial achievements — she writes him in a dialect that is thick enough to feel authentic but never so thick it becomes a barrier.
And his philosophical position is stated with such absolute confidence.
He says, and I want to read this exactly:
'I believe what I see, and no more. That's what I believe, young woman. I don't believe all I hear—no! not by a big deal.'
The repetition of 'I believe' three times in rapid succession — that is someone nailing their creed to the door.
But what follows immediately is the tenderest possible evidence that his materialism is not hard-heartedness — quite the opposite.
He has been watching Bessy flush with anticipation every time she heard a strange step at the door — waiting for Margaret to come.
'And my wench here thought a deal about it, and flushed up many a time, when hoo little knew as I was looking at her.'
He has been secretly watching his dying daughter hope. That is devastating.
That detail of Higgins watching Bessy without her knowing — it's the most economical piece of characterisation.
He's a man who says he only believes what he sees — and what he sees is his child's secret joy.
And he has kept that to himself, and watches it, and it clearly matters to him enormously.
He ends by welcoming Margaret — warmly — but with the condition that she keep 'from preaching on what hoo knows nought about.'
It's funny, and it's fair, and it sets the terms of a relationship that becomes one of the novel's great friendships.
What strikes me about Higgins is the rhythm of his speech — Gaskell writes dialect prose that actually has comic timing built into it.
That 'no! not by a big deal' — the exclamation, the pause before the negation — you can hear the man perform himself.
He knows he's a character. He leans into it.
And yet the love for Bessy underneath it is completely unperformed. It's just there, in the observation.
Let's move from the working-class north to the drawing rooms of the educated south — specifically to Mr. Bell, one of the novel's most intriguing presences.
Eleanor, you have two passages with Bell — one where he explodes at Thornton over how he speaks about Margaret, and another where Margaret herself reflects on time and change at Helstone.
What does Bell reveal about the novel's emotional intelligence when he gets angry?
Bell is furious in that scene, and the fury is completely earned.
Thornton has referred to Margaret as simply 'a beautiful creature' — reducing her to an aesthetic object — and Bell detonates.
The passage is worth reading in full:
'Is that all! You can speak of her in that measured way, as simply a beautiful creature—only something to catch the eye.'
And then Bell makes this astonishing moral claim:
'to have loved her without return would have lifted you higher than all those, be they who they may, that have ever known her to love.'
That is a completely counter-intuitive argument — unrequited love as moral elevation rather than humiliation.
Bell is saying that Margaret is so extraordinary that even failing to win her would have been a form of grace.
It's a romantic argument dressed in the language of virtue, and it's devastating because Gaskell clearly means it.
And Bell ends by asking Thornton: 'Do you speak of her as you would of a horse or a dog?'
Which is wonderful — because it's the most undignified possible comparison, and Bell delivers it with the full force of his dignity.
Gaskell gives him that line as a kind of moral thunderclap, and then gets out of the way.
She doesn't editorialize. She doesn't tell us Thornton is chastened.
She just lets Bell's question hang in the air and trusts the reader to feel its weight.
Bell's rage on Margaret's behalf is one of the most moving things in the novel for me, precisely because it's unexpected from him.
He presents as the jovial Oxford don, the man who takes nothing too seriously — and then suddenly this erupts.
It tells you that his affection for Margaret — this godfather-like love — is the most serious thing about him.
And the tragedy is that he's dying. He will not live to see what becomes of her.
Which makes the Helstone passage — Chapter Forty-Six — feel almost unbearable in retrospect.
Margaret visits the place of her childhood — not to recapture it, but to discover that it has changed irrevocably.
And Gaskell allows her this great extended meditation on time, change, and death.
The passage builds through the domestic — households changed by 'absence, or death, or marriage' — and then opens out into something vast.

She writes of 'the natural mutations brought by days and months and years, which carry us on imperceptibly from childhood to youth, and thence through manhood to age, whence we drop like fruit, fully ripe, into the quiet mother earth.'
'Drop like fruit, fully ripe, into the quiet mother earth' — that is not the language of lamentation.
That is acceptance — a kind of earned pastoral calm — which makes it more devastating than any wailing could be.
And Bell is asleep in the corner while she thinks all of this.
That small, ordinary detail — the old man sleeping after exercise — set beside her enormous meditation on mortality.
It's the Gaskell method at its best: the sublime and the quotidian occupying the same room, neither one diminishing the other.
And then the tea-tray arrives, carried by a flushed country girl who's been helping in the hay-field.
Life just continues. It always does.
The road that has been 'trimmed and narrowed' and the 'green straggling pathway' enclosed and cultivated — Gaskell calls it 'a great improvement.'
'A great improvement it was called' — and then Margaret sighs over the loss.
'It was called' — passive construction, gently ironic, quietly devastating.
The narrator doesn't argue with progress. She simply notes who decides what counts as improvement, and who mourns what's lost.
That is North and South's entire argument, in microcosm, conducted in a hedgerow.
That feels like exactly the right note on which to pause — the novel's argument conducted in a hedgerow.
We've traced today how Gaskell uses narrative distance — not as coldness, but as a kind of moral precision.

The child suppressing her tears to protect her father, the man watching his dying daughter hope, the woman meditating on mortality while an old friend sleeps — all of it told with the lightest possible narrative touch.
My deepest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has, I think, done justice to a truly great novel.
Join us for the next segment of North and South Unpacked.

segments.title: Closing: Love, Class, and the Cost of Understanding

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing Margaret Hale and John Thornton across the full arc of North and South.
What I want to do in this closing segment is sit with what the novel earns — and what it costs.
We have a moment of raw, unguarded confession. We have a man remaking himself in failure. And we have an ending that chooses silence over declaration.
Eleanor, Oliver, Caroline — let's bring it home.
I want to begin with the scene in the dining room — because I think it's one of the most technically daring passages in the novel.
Gaskell has been careful, throughout, to keep Thornton's inner life at arm's length — we see him through Margaret's resistance, through his mother's devotion, through his public conduct.
And then, when Margaret falls unconscious in his arms, all of that armour simply drops away.
Gaskell tells us: the sense of what she was to him came upon him so keenly that he spoke it out in his pain.
"Oh, my Margaret—my Margaret! no one can tell what you are to me! Dead—cold as you lie there, you are the only woman I ever loved!"
He says it because she cannot hear him. That's the structural genius of the moment.
It is the confession of a man speaking into what he believes is a void — and it tells us everything the novel has been building toward.
When I recorded that passage, I had to stop before I reached those words and simply sit with the page for a moment.
Because what Gaskell has done — and it is extraordinarily calculated — is chosen the vocative. Not 'Margaret.' Not even 'Miss Hale.'
"My Margaret." Twice. With the possessive that he has absolutely no right to claim.
And the rhythm of it — "Dead—cold as you lie there" — that em dash does so much work.
It's not a comma. It's a catch in the throat. The prose performs the emotion rather than describing it.
And then — and then — his mother's voice is about to be heard. The public world rushes back in, and he has to seal himself up again.
What undoes me every time is how brief it is.
She falls. He catches her. He speaks. And within moments, the world has returned and it is as though nothing happened — except that we know.
Gaskell gives us a window into his soul, and then she closes the shutter.
And that restraint carries forward, I think, all the way to the ending — to that scene where they are finally together.
Gaskell writes simply: "He clasped her close. But they both kept silence."
After everything — all the argument, the class friction, the misunderstanding, the grief — she gives them silence.
It's the most intimate thing she could have written.
And what makes the silence possible — what makes the reunion bearable — is what happens to Thornton in Chapter 51.
He has failed. The mill is gone. The position of master — the identity he built himself into — is relinquished.
And in that loss, something opens in him. He tells Colthurst exactly what he wants from his next employment.
"My only wish is to have the opportunity of cultivating some intercourse with the hands beyond the mere 'cash nexus.'"
This is the man Margaret once dismissed as a mere tradesman. He has become something harder to dismiss.
He has turned his failure into a philosophical programme — and Gaskell asks us to see that as growth, not consolation.
The 'cash nexus' line is doing something quite remarkable, because it's a political term — Carlyle's term — being used by a Milton manufacturer who has just been ruined.
He is not using the language of sentiment. He is using the language of social critique — applied to himself and his own industry.
And then Gaskell allows him this lovely, dry aside — that other manufacturers shake their heads and look grave when he mentions these experiments.
He is not naive. He knows exactly how outlandish he sounds to his peers. And he doesn't care.
He has, in a sense, become more like Margaret — or rather, he has become the person that Margaret's challenge always asked him to be.
And Margaret, of course, has moved too. She has come to understand industry, commerce, the North — on its own terms.
So when they clasp each other in silence at the end, it is not a surrender by either of them.
It is recognition. Two people who have earned each other.
That feels like the right place to let the novel rest.
North and South is a novel about the cost of understanding — the work required to see past class, past pride, past the story we tell ourselves about who we are.
Gaskell earns her ending because she never makes it easy. The silences, the misreadings, the moments of raw confession that go unheard — they are all the price of admission.
My thanks to Dr. Eleanor Hartley, to Oliver Trevelyan, and to Caroline Woodcourt — for bringing this novel alive with such intelligence and care.
This has been North and South Unpacked. Thank you for listening.

She looked out upon the dark-grey lines of the church towers, square and
straight in the centre of the view, cutting against the deep blue
transparent depths beyond, into which she gazed, and felt that she might
gaze for ever, seeing at every moment some farther distance, and yet no
sign of God! It seemed to her at the moment, as if the earth was more
utterly desolate than if girt in by an iron dome, behind which there
might be the ineffaceable peace and glory of the Almighty: those
never-ending depths of space, in their still serenity, were more mocking
to her than any material bounds could be—shutting in the cries of
earth’s sufferers, which now might ascend into that infinite splendour
of vastness and be lost—lost for ever, before they reached His throne.
In this mood her father came in unheard. The moonlight was strong enough
to let him see his daughter in her unusual place and attitude. He came
to her and touched her shoulder before she was aware that he was there.
c5:p8.summary: Margaret gazes at the night sky in despair, unable to discern God's presence; her father silently enters and asks her to pray with him.

c7:p27.text:
Margaret could not help her looks; but the short curled upper lip, the
round, massive up-turned chin, the manner of carrying her head, her
movements, full of a soft feminine defiance, always gave strangers the
impression of haughtiness. She was tired now, and would much rather have
remained silent, and taken the rest her father had planned for her; but,
of course, she owed to herself to be a gentlewoman, and to speak
courteously from time to time to this stranger; not over-brushed, nor
over-polished, it must be confessed, after his rough encounter with
Milton streets and crowds. She wished that he would go, as he had once
spoken of doing, instead of sitting there, answering with curt sentences
all the remarks she made. She had taken off her shawl, and hung it over
the back of her chair. She sat facing him and facing the light; her full
beauty met his eye; her round white flexile throat rising out of the
full, yet lithe figure; her lips moving so slightly as she spoke, not
breaking the cold serene look of her face with any variation from the
one lovely haughty curve; her eyes, with their soft gloom, meeting his
with quiet maiden freedom. He almost said to himself that he did not
like her, before their conversation ended; he tried so to compensate
himself for the mortified feeling, that while he looked upon her with
an admiration he could not repress, she looked at him with proud
indifference, taking him, he thought, for what, in his irritation, he
told himself he was—a great rough fellow, with not a grace or a
refinement about him. Her quiet coldness of demeanour he interpreted
into contemptuousness, and resented it in his heart to the pitch of
almost inclining him to get up and go away, and have nothing more to do
with these Hales, and their superciliousness.
c7:p27.summary: Margaret struggles to maintain courteous conversation with the tired Thornton, whom she wishes would leave; Thornton interprets her cool, dignified bearing as haughtiness and contempt, and becomes increasingly resentful, nearly leaving in irritation at her apparent indifference to him.

“Oh, papa! you don’t mean that you thought me so silly? I really liked
that account of himself better than anything else he said. Everything
else revolted me, from its hardness; but he spoke about himself so
simply—with so little of the pretence that makes the vulgarity of
shop-people, and with such tender respect for his mother, that I was
less likely to leave the room then than when he was boasting about
Milton, as if there was not such another place in the world; or quietly
professing to despise people for careless, wasteful improvidence,
without ever seeming to think it his duty to try to make them
different,—to give them anything of the training which his mother gave
him, and to which he evidently owes his position, whatever that may be.
No! his statement of having been a shop-boy was the thing I liked best
of all.”

It appeared to Mr. Thornton that all these graceful cares were habitual
to the family; and especially of a piece with Margaret. She stood by the
tea-table in a light-coloured muslin gown, which had a good deal of pink
about it. She looked as if she was not attending to the conversation,
but solely busy with the tea-cups, among which her round ivory hands
moved with pretty, noiseless, daintiness. She had a bracelet on one
taper arm, which would fall down over her round wrist. Mr. Thornton
watched the replacing of this troublesome ornament with far more
attention than he listened to her father. It seemed as if it fascinated
him to see her push it up impatiently until it tightened her soft flesh;
and then to mark the loosening—the fall. He could almost have
exclaimed—“There it goes again!” There was so little left to be done
after he arrived at the preparation for tea, that he was almost sorry
the obligation of eating and drinking came so soon to prevent him
watching Margaret. She handed him his cup of tea with the proud air of
an unwilling slave; but her eye caught the moment when he was ready for
another cup; and he almost longed to ask her to do for him what he saw
her compelled to do for her father, who took her little finger and thumb
in his masculine hand, and made them serve as sugar-tongues. Mr.
Thornton saw her beautiful eyes lifted to her father, full of light,
half-laughter, and half-love, as this bit of pantomime went on between
the two, unobserved as they fancied, by any. Margaret’s head still
ached, as the paleness of her complexion, and her silence might have
testified; but she was resolved to throw herself into the breach, if
there was any long untoward pause, rather than that her father’s friend,
pupil, and guest should have cause to think himself in any way
neglected. But the conversation went on; and Margaret drew into a
corner, near her mother, with her work, after the tea-things were taken
away; and felt that she might let her thoughts roam, without fear of
being suddenly wanted to fill up a gap.
c10:p2.summary: Thornton watches Margaret serve tea with fascination, noting her grace and composure, while she strives to fulfil her duty as hostess despite a headache and her initial coldness toward him.
